_comment: English overrides for phases.content.ts / diagnostics.content.ts. EMPTY ON PURPOSE FOR NOW: the content translation is sequenced after the output-analyser work lands in those two files, so this file ships as the wired-up, verified mechanism and nothing else. Shape (see content-i18n.ts, which is the type-level source of truth): { "phases": { "<phase.id>": { "title", "why", "stopGate", "paste": { "<index>": { "label" } }, "checks": { "<check.id>": { "label", "failFix": { "<index>": { "when", "note" } } } } } }, "symptoms": { "<symptom.id>": { "seen", "causes": { "<index>": { "tell", "cause", "note" } } } }, "assertions": { "<check.id>": { "fallback", "rules": { "<index>": { "why" } } } } }. There is deliberately NO key for command, expect, assert, script, probe or fix -- those must stay byte-identical in every locale, and the absence of a key is what makes that true rather than a rule someone has to remember. scripts/check-guided-i18n.mjs enforces the rest.

audit.title: Is the router clean
audit.why: If old provisioning is left behind, the new settings stack on top of it and the wrong org/location IDs keep running.
audit.stopGate: If the counts are not all 0, stop and reset. Build on top of an old config and guests will land on the old portal, and you will lose hours debugging it.

0.label: Router audit — find any old config

audit-clean.label: No old Wyfy config left on the router
audit-clean.expectLabel: all seven counts 0: hotspot-count=0, radius-count=0, wireguard-count=0, apiuser-count=0, cert-count=0, file-count=0, firewall-count=0 -- and not a single cloudguest-file line

0.whenLabel: any count came back higher than 0
0.note: The router will reboot and your connection will drop — that is normal. Wait 2 minutes, reconnect in WinBox by MAC, and run this audit again. All the counts should be 0 now.

1.whenLabel: file-count is higher than 0, e.g. flash/cloudguest-hotspot/
1.note: That is a folder left over from the July provisioning. It holds portal links carrying the old org/location/router IDs, which will still send guests to the wrong place today. Deleting the files is not enough — do a full reset.

2.whenLabel: Still cannot find the router after the reset
2.note: Put the laptop cable into ether2 (not ether1 — that one is for the internet). Open WinBox, click the MAC address in the 'Neighbors' tab, log in as admin with a blank password.

clock.title: Internet and the clock
clock.why: The hEX has no battery-backed clock — every power cut leaves it on the wrong date, and on a wrong date both the heartbeat scheduler and HTTPS fail silently.
clock.stopGate: If the date is not today's, stop. The router will configure fine on a wrong date but will show as offline in the Master console forever — and that is very hard to catch later.

clock-internet.label: The internet is working
clock-internet.expectLabel: RESULT: PASS -- the internet is working

0.note: The ISP cable belongs in ether1 and the laptop in ether2. Do not swap them. Plug it in, wait 30 seconds, and run the block again.
NTP needs the internet. Get the ping above to PASS first, then run this command and check /system clock print again 10 seconds later.

1.note: Set the date by hand (today's date). That is temporary but enough — NTP will correct it later on its own. Do not move on with a wrong date.

wan.title: WAN and route repair
wan.why: The script reads the gateway immediately after creating the DHCP client — the lease has not arrived yet, so the route is built with gateway 0.0.0.0 and the whole internet goes down.
wan.stopGate: If the route is not As, do not move on at all — the hotspot, the tunnel and RADIUS all run over this route, and all three will fail silently.

0.label: Wait for the DHCP lease + repair the route (always run this after the script)

wan-lease.label: An address came through from the ISP

0.note: Is the ISP cable seated properly in ether1? Is the ISP's own router powered on? Unplug the cable, plug it back in, and look again 30 seconds later.

wan-route-active.label: The default route is ACTIVE, not inactive

0.whenLabel: flags show Is, or the GATEWAY column is 0.0.0.0
0.note: This is exactly the bug. The route was created but the gateway was empty. After you run this the route becomes As and ping starts working.

1.note: That means the lease still has not arrived. Wait 30 seconds and run the repair block above again — re-running it is completely safe.

gate.title: The real gate to the internet
gate.stopGate: If it does not come back PASS, stop. Everything past this point needs the internet, and some of it will fail silently with no error at all.

0.label: Test the internet and DNS together

gate-pass.label: Both the internet and DNS are working

0.note: The script sets the DNS servers in a later chunk, so running this check before that gives a false FAIL. Run this command and run the gate again — it will PASS now. The router was fine all along.

1.note: Go back to Phase 2 — whether the route is As or Is is the real problem.

hotspot.title: LAN and hotspot
hotspot.why: After you paste the Master console's LAN and Hotspot chunks, three settings are left over that the script does not set.
hotspot.stopGate: All four checks have to PASS. If any one of them is wrong the guest will log in and believe everything worked, while nothing actually does.

0.label: Hotspot hardening (run after the LAN + Hotspot chunks)

1.label: Hotspot audit — is every setting right?

hs-idle.label: Sessions close themselves (otherwise sessions pile up)

0.note: With keepalive off, idle-timeout is the only backstop left. Leave it at none and sessions never close, the data cap never applies, and the active list keeps growing.

hs-loginby.label: The router will accept the login form
hs-loginby.commandLabel: (the login-by line in the audit block)

0.note: cookie,http-chap is the RouterOS default, and the portal's form cannot satisfy it -- CHAP needs a challenge/response the guest page never fetches. The guest will enter the right OTP, nothing will happen, and nothing will appear in the router's log either. Set http-pap only; do not add https.

1.note: https puts a certificate warning on the guest's phone -- the router stands up TLS with its own self-signed certificate, which no browser trusts. The guest gets a full-screen security warning before ever seeing the portal, and the OTP is posted to that same untrusted endpoint, so the gate never opens. http-pap has to stand alone.

hs-shared.label: One guest can use two devices (phone + laptop)
hs-shared.commandLabel: (the shared-users line in the audit block)

0.note: At 1, the guest's laptop gets 'no more sessions are allowed for user' — and that is not a soft error, the whole login fails.

hs-guest.label: The local guest user is disabled (no portal bypass)

0.note: The router checks its own local user first and RADIUS second. So anyone who knows the guest password can bypass the portal completely — no OTP, no record, no data cap. That password is printed on the Master console screen, which makes this a real risk.

portal.title: The path to the portal
portal.why: Without the walled garden a guest's browser cannot reach the portal at all — a captive portal blocks even its own server.
portal.stopGate: If the walled-garden ip list stays empty no guest will ever be able to open the portal — and no error will show anywhere on the router. Never skip this check.

0.label: Walled garden — set both lists (this one reports its own FAIL)

1.label: Where are the portal files, and are they right?

wg-ip.label: The portal's IP is in the HTTPS list (this is what breaks most often)

0.note: Run the walled garden block above again. If it still reports FAIL, run the Phase 3 DNS fix (/ip dns set servers=8.8.8.8,1.1.1.1 allow-remote-requests=yes) and then this block. With DNS broken this block sets nothing at all, silently — which is why you must not skip this check.

1.note: The portal's IP must have changed. Run the block above again — it updates the old entry rather than creating a duplicate.

wg-host.label: The HTTP list is set too

0.note: The two lists are different things — the HTTP one is only for http, the IP one for https. You need both.

portal-files.label: The portal's redirect pages are on the router

0.note: The five 'Portal Redirect Page' chunks from the Master console have not been pasted yet. Paste them, then run this check again.

1.whenLabel: the file exists but is small / $(link-login-only) is missing
1.note: The script assumes the path flash/hotspot/login.html, but on some models the path is just hotspot/login.html. When that happens the paste runs, no error appears, and the file never changes. Send whatever real path the block above printed to the Master console team — they will have to change it.

2.whenLabel: the guest sees the blue MikroTik login page instead of the Wyfy portal
2.note: That is the visible symptom of the problem above. The router is fine, the redirect page just never got uploaded.

cert-optional.label: The certificate chunk (optional — you can skip it)

0.whenLabel: 'input does not match any value of ca' error
0.note: That is an old bug in the chunk. Run this command to clean up and skip the certificate chunk — the guest portal works fully without it, because the walled-garden path never touches the hotspot's certificate.

tunnel.title: Tunnel and RADIUS
tunnel.why: To verify an OTP the router has to reach the hub through the tunnel — with the tunnel down, a guest's OTP will sit on a spinner forever.
tunnel.stopGate: If ping does not reach the hub, a guest's OTP will never verify — the spinner just keeps going and the guest concludes the app is broken.

0.label: Fix the firewall order + the RADIUS src-address (after the WireGuard/RADIUS chunks)

1.label: Are the tunnel and RADIUS alive?

2.label: Does the heartbeat scheduler exist? (this is what makes the dashboard go live)

tunnel-up.label: Ping reaches the hub through the tunnel
tunnel-up.expectLabel: RESULT: PASS -- we reached the hub

0.whenLabel: last-handshake is very old or blank
0.note: The most common cause: the firewall's allow rule ended up BELOW the drop rule, so the tunnel's own replies get blocked. This command lifts it above. The handshake should appear within 30 seconds.

1.whenLabel: RESULT: FAIL -- there is no RADIUS entry
1.note: The Master console's RADIUS chunk was never pasted. Note the order: RADIUS needs WireGuard first, so paste the two chunks in order.

hb-scheduler.label: The heartbeat scheduler exists (this is what makes the router show as live in Master console)

0.whenLabel: RESULT: FAIL -- koi cloudguest scheduler nahi hai, heartbeat kabhi nahi jayega
0.note: The Heartbeat chunk was never pasted, or the paste died partway. In a single-line paste one syntax error silently abandons EVERYTHING after it, and RouterOS still reports success. Look at the `### cloudguest` markers at the end of the generated script -- the last line should be COMPLETE. If it stopped at `START 9/14`, paste again from there. Skipping this chunk means the router works but the dashboard shows provisioning forever.

1.whenLabel: sched count is above 0 but next-run is blank
1.note: The scheduler exists but will never fire. The usual cause is the router's clock -- go back to the date check in Phase 2. The hEX has no battery-backed clock, so the date is wrong after every power cut and the scheduler's start-time is filled in against that wrong date.

radius-counters.label: The RADIUS counters (look at these after a guest test)

0.note: The packet is not reaching the hub at all — run the tunnel check again.

1.note: It is reaching the hub, but the secret does not match. Do NOT press Generate again in the Master console — follow the Phase 8 recovery instead.

2.note: A reply is coming back but the router is rejecting it. That is a server-side problem, not the router's — tell the team.

phonetest.title: The real test, from a phone
phonetest.why: Every check on the router can pass and the guest experience can still be broken — only a real phone tells you the truth.
phonetest.stopGate: Do not treat the router as live until this phase passes. Everything else can pass and it can still fail on a real phone.

0.label: Watch it live — did the guest connect or not

phone-mobiledata.label: Mobile data is OFF on the phone
phone-mobiledata.commandLabel: (turn mobile data off in the phone's settings, then connect to the WiFi)
phone-mobiledata.expectLabel: Mobile data off — otherwise the phone quietly uses 4G and the test passes for the wrong reason

0.whenLabel: the test looks like it passed but you are not sure
0.note: Never run this test without mobile data off. The phone slips onto 4G in the background and you think the WiFi is working.

phone-portal.label: The portal opens by itself
phone-portal.commandLabel: (connect to the WiFi; the portal should open on its own)
phone-portal.expectLabel: The Wyfy portal sign-in page — not the blue MikroTik page

0.note: Open the browser's ADDRESS BAR and type: wifi.wyfyguest.com — in the address bar, not the search box. That takes you straight to the portal.

1.whenLabel: the blue MikroTik login page opened
1.note: The portal's redirect pages are not on the router. Go back to the portal-files check in Phase 5.

2.whenLabel: the page never loaded / timed out
2.note: The walled-garden ip list is probably empty. Run the first block of Phase 5 again.

phone-otp.label: The OTP login works
phone-otp.commandLabel: (enter your own real number, then the OTP)
phone-otp.expectLabel: After logging in you should see the connected/session screen

0.whenLabel: the spinner keeps going after entering the OTP
0.note: Run the Phase 6 tunnel check — is ping reaching the hub or not.

1.whenLabel: login succeeded and the internet works, but 'session expired' appeared straight away
1.note: That is NOT an expiry. The guest's browser is blocking storage (the iPhone WiFi login window, or private browsing). The internet working means the router has done its whole job. This is a known app-side problem — tell the team, change nothing on the router.

phone-realsite.label: Real internet works after logging in
phone-realsite.commandLabel: (open some new https site you have never opened before)

0.whenLabel: the portal opened but everything else is blocked
0.note: If your phone shows up here, the router has accepted the login. If it does not show up, the login never completed.

phone-reconnect.label: Turn WiFi off/on and reconnect
phone-reconnect.commandLabel: (turn the phone's WiFi off, wait 10 seconds, turn it back on)
phone-reconnect.expectLabel: Either it just works, or the portal opens again and you log in

0.whenLabel: after reconnecting it says 'connected' but there is no internet
0.note: That is an old known bug which has already been fixed. If it still happens, tell the team — it is the portal app's problem, not the router's.

recovery.title: Something has gone wrong
recovery.why: The moment you press Generate again in the Master console every secret changes, while the router keeps the old ones — and that fails silently.
recovery.stopGate: With a secret mismatch the guests keep working but the Master console cannot control the router — so do not file this under 'we will look at it later'.

0.label: Is there a secret mismatch? (check this first)

1.label: Reset the secrets only (the rest of the router's config survives)

2.label: Full factory reset (when nothing else makes sense)

0.note: Run this command again.
Remove them all and paste the RADIUS chunk exactly once. With two entries the router can keep trying the wrong one.

1.whenLabel: the log still shows login failures
1.note: Do NOT press Generate again in the Master console. Use the script that was already generated — every Generate mints new secrets and brings the problem straight back.

rec-full.label: The router is reachable after the factory reset

0.note: Wait 2 minutes. Laptop cable into ether2. WinBox → Neighbors tab → click the MAC. Log in as admin with a blank password. Then start again from Phase 0.

wan-no-route-to-host.seen: Ping anything from the router and you get "no route to host", even though `/ip route print` shows a 0.0.0.0/0 line.

0.tell: Flags show `Is` (I = inactive) and the line has `gateway=0.0.0.0`.
0.cause: The script ran through `/import`. `/import` never pauses -- the lease's gateway was read microseconds after the DHCP client was added, the lease had not arrived yet, so the route was built with gateway `0.0.0.0` and is permanently Inactive.
0.note: This is a live fix, already proven. It never happens on a chunk-by-chunk terminal paste, because human typing delay gives DHCP time to bind -- it only shows up on an `.rsc` `/import`. After the fix the flag should become `As`.

1.tell: Flags show `Is` but `gateway=` holds a real IP (e.g. `gateway=192.168.2.1`).
1.cause: The gateway is written correctly but it is not answering ping, so `check-gateway=ping` marked the route inactive itself. That means the WAN cable/ISP link is genuinely down.
1.note: `status: no-link` means a cable/port problem; `status: link-ok` with ping failing means the ISP's side. This is not a route bug -- the moment the gateway is healthy RouterOS turns the route `As` by itself, no command needed.

2.tell: The command prints nothing at all -- there is no 0.0.0.0/0 line.
2.cause: The WAN Routing chunk never created the route, because the gateway was blank at the time (DHCP had not bound, or PPPoE had not connected). The chunk does not error, it skips silently.
2.note: First confirm `/ip dhcp-client print detail` reports `status: bound`, otherwise pasting again gives you the same blank gateway. The heartbeat scheduler retries this every 5 minutes too, so you can also just wait 5 min and look again.

3.tell: Flags show `As` (A = active) and `gateway=` holds a real IP -- the route is perfectly fine.
3.cause: There is no routing problem. It showed up as `no route to host` by name, but the real trouble is in DNS or the firewall.
3.note: If `8.8.8.8` pings but names do not resolve, go to the `dns-servers-empty` symptom. With an `As` route, stop blaming the WAN.

wan-dhcp-client-not-bound.seen: The cable is in the WAN port but the router is getting no IP from upstream at all -- the WAN Connectivity Check reports FAIL.

0.cause: The router is sending DHCP requests and upstream is not answering. Either the cable is in the wrong port, or DHCP is off on the upstream router/ONT.
0.note: `status: no-link` means cable/port; with `link-ok` and still `searching`, the upstream DHCP server is not replying -- get the venue's ISP box checked.

1.tell: `status: bound` and `gateway=` holds a real IP.
1.cause: DHCP is perfectly fine. The trouble is in routing or DNS, not in addressing.
1.note: Copy the `gateway=` value from here and apply the `wan-no-route-to-host` fix directly -- in 90% of cases that is the one thing left over after an `.rsc` import.

2.tell: The command gives empty output -- there is no dhcp-client entry at all.
2.cause: Either the venue is on a static IP (the script was generated in static mode), or the WAN Addressing chunk was never pasted.
2.note: If you see a static address there with the comment `cloudguest-addr-wan1`, this is a static venue -- the ISP supplied the gateway, it will never arrive over DHCP, and in that case the route's gateway was hardcoded at generate time. If there is nothing there either, paste the WAN Addressing chunk.

3.tell: `status: bound` but the `gateway=` line is missing / empty.
3.cause: Upstream handed out an address but sent no default gateway option -- a cheap or misconfigured upstream router. Very rare.
3.note: Usually the upstream's LAN IP is the `.1` of the same subnet your lease came from. This is a one-off manual step; there is no automatic fix for it.

wan-pppoe-not-connected.seen: The venue is on PPPoE (BSNL/JioFiber type), the script pasted fine but there is no internet -- the default route was never created.

0.tell: `status: connected` and `remote-address:` holds a real IP.
0.cause: The PPPoE session is up. The route is missing only because the WAN Routing chunk ran while the session was still negotiating.
0.note: `remote-address` is the real next hop (the ISP's BRAS). On PPPoE never look at `/ip dhcp-client`, there will be nothing there.

1.cause: It is reaching the PPPoE server but no session forms -- usually the ONT/modem is still dialling PPPoE itself, and the ISP allows only one session.
1.note: Dialling one PPPoE account from two places is the single most common field mistake. Kill the session on the modem and the router connects within seconds.

2.tell: Stuck on `status: authenticating`, or `authentication failed` in the log.
2.cause: The PPPoE username/password typed at Generate time is wrong.
2.note: Fix it by hand here -- do not click Generate again, that rotates the WireGuard and RADIUS secrets and bricks the router.

3.tell: The command errors with `no such item`.
3.cause: The pppoe-client interface was never created -- the WAN Addressing chunk was not pasted.
3.note: Order matters: the pppoe interface has to exist first, only then can the routing chunk read its gateway.

double-nat-private-wan-ip.seen: The WAN port got a private IP like `192.168.2.199/24` instead of a public one -- it looks like something went wrong.

0.cause: This is double NAT -- our router sits behind an upstream router. For a captive portal that is completely normal and it is how 95% of venues are.
0.note: Do nothing about it. The guest's traffic is NAT'd twice, that is all -- the portal, OTP, RADIUS, WireGuard and the bandwidth queue all work fine through it. It only breaks things if someone needs a port-forward into the router from the outside internet (i.e. WinBox/SSH remotely) -- and we never do that, we come in over the WireGuard tunnel. Do not waste time on this.

1.cause: The ISP is doing CGNAT (carrier-grade NAT) itself. That is also fine for us, though upstream UDP filtering is more common here.
1.note: If the WireGuard handshake is not happening, see the `wg-handshake-missing` symptom -- ISP UDP blocking turns up most often on CGNAT connections.

2.tell: `address=` holds a real public IP (not in a private range).
2.cause: The router is connected straight to the ISP; there is no double NAT at all.
2.note: Nothing to do here either. Just be aware the router is now directly exposed to the internet, so the Firewall chunk must have been pasted (`cloudguest-fw-drop-wan-input` should be present).

3.cause: There is no address on that interface at all -- the WAN has not come up.
3.note: Go to `wan-dhcp-client-not-bound`. This is not a double NAT question.

dns-servers-empty.seen: The router can ping `8.8.8.8` but no website opens on a guest's phone -- "server not found".

0.tell: The `servers:` line is empty (nothing written after it).
0.cause: The router has no upstream resolver at all. Our DHCP client runs with `use-peer-dns=no` (deliberately), so the ISP's DNS never arrives on its own -- and the DHCP server hands guests `10.5.50.1`, i.e. the router itself. If the router cannot resolve anything, neither can the guest.
0.note: This is the single most repeated failure in the whole setup. `allow-remote-requests=yes` is essential, otherwise guests cannot even ask the router. After fixing it, be sure to check `walled-garden-https-entry-missing` too -- broken DNS may well have stopped that entry being created either.

1.cause: The resolver is set but the router cannot reach it -- that is a WAN/route problem, not a DNS one.
1.note: If ping fails too, go to `wan-no-route-to-host`. Trying one DNS server after another is pointless here.

2.cause: The router resolves fine for itself but rejects the guests' queries -- DHCP gave them `10.5.50.1` and the door there is shut.
2.note: `:resolve` works on the router but nothing opens on the guest's phone -- that is exactly this combination. Do not blame the WAN for it.

3.cause: DNS is perfectly fine. The trouble is further on -- in the walled garden or in hotspot L2.

walled-garden-https-entry-missing.seen: The guest joins the WiFi, the login page even appears, but the portal never opens / white screen / timeout.

0.tell: There is no line with `comment="cloudguest-portal-https"` at all.
0.cause: That entry is built at paste time from an on-device `:resolve`, and its `on-error` only writes a warning to the log. So: DNS was broken at paste time -> the entry was never created, and no error was ever shown. The guest is left with no route to an HTTPS portal.
0.note: This ONE failure puts the entire guest portal out of reach while everything else on the router looks green. Fix DNS first, then run this -- do it the other way round and the entry still will not be created. Or just paste the Walled Garden chunk again, it will resolve properly now.

1.tell: `comment="cloudguest-portal-https"` exists but `dst-address=` holds an old/wrong IP.
1.cause: The portal's IP has changed (a host or CDN move) and the old one is pinned on the device.
1.note: Pasting the Walled Garden chunk again updates this too -- it is set-if-present, not add-if-missing. Confirm the new IP matches the one `:resolve` returns.

2.tell: The entry exists, `dst-address=` is right, and `action=accept` is set.
2.cause: The walled garden is fine. The trouble is in the guest's DNS or in hotspot L2.
2.note: Check one more thing: `/ip hotspot walled-garden print detail` (a separate, host-based table) should hold a `cloudguest-portal` entry -- that one is needed for the HTTP redirect, the IP one for HTTPS. They are two different mechanisms.

portal-never-loads.seen: The guest is on the WiFi but the portal page never appears at all -- no login page, no error, just a spinner or a timeout.

0.tell: `status: finished` / `downloaded: ...KiB` -- the router itself reached the portal.
0.cause: The router's WAN and DNS are both fine. So the guest's path is what is blocked -- the walled garden's HTTPS entry is missing.
0.note: This is the most time-consuming lookalike there is -- everything works from the router, nothing works for the guest. The full detail is in `walled-garden-https-entry-missing`.

1.tell: `failure: dns name does not exist` or `resolving failed`.
1.cause: The router has no DNS at all -- `/ip dns` will have empty servers.
1.note: Right after fixing DNS, get the walled-garden entry created as well -- it will have been skipped at paste time because of that same broken DNS.

2.cause: The WAN/route is down. The name resolved but the packet is not getting out.
2.note: Go to `wan-no-route-to-host`. Blaming the walled garden or the portal here is pointless.

3.tell: `status: finished` comes back and the walled-garden entry is present too.
3.cause: The network side is clean. Either the guest's traffic is not reaching the router, or the guest's phone is not triggering the portal at all.
3.note: Now go to `guests-get-nothing` (L2/DHCP). A self-signed certificate warning interstitial also eats the guest's URL params -- if a cert warning appeared on the phone, this is not a network issue.

wg-handshake-missing.seen: The dashboard shows the router "offline" or WireGuard "not connected", while you are sitting in front of the router and the internet works.

0.tell: There is no `last-handshake=` line (or the value is blank), and `tx=` is climbing while `rx=0 B`.
0.cause: Our packets are going out and nothing is coming back from the hub. Usually the upstream ISP blocks UDP egress (common on managed hotel/mall connections), or there is no path to the endpoint.
0.note: If ICMP ping works but `rx=0 B` stays put, the ISP is blocking UDP/51820 -- that is not fixable on the router, you have to talk to the venue's ISP or add a second uplink. It only breaks remote management; the guests' portal and internet are not affected.

1.tell: Both `tx=0 B` and `rx=0 B`, and no `last-handshake=` either.
1.cause: The router has not sent a single packet -- either the peer is wrong/incomplete, or there is no IP address on the tunnel interface.
1.note: `endpoint-address=20.219.72.235`, `endpoint-port=51820`, `persistent-keepalive=25s` and `10.20.0.x/24` on the tunnel -- all four have to be there. If even one is missing, paste the WireGuard Tunnel chunk again. Do not click Generate again: that rotates the keys, and since the chunk is add-if-missing, a re-paste will NOT repair it either.

2.cause: `wg-cloudguard` is the correct name -- the generator and the backend both create it. `wg-cloudguest` is the legacy name, left behind on routers provisioned before that fix. Both exist here, and the firewall rule is tied to only one of them, so traffic can be going over the other.
2.note: First run `print detail` and see which one actually has a real `last-handshake=`. Normally you keep `wg-cloudguard` and remove the older `wg-cloudguest`. If the handshake is on `wg-cloudguest` instead, remove nothing -- that router is running on the old name, so re-provision it from the Advanced panel. The firewall rule's `in-interface=` has to match the name of the surviving tunnel.

3.tell: A recent value like `last-handshake=1m30s` is showing.
3.cause: The handshake is happening. The tunnel is up -- this symptom ends here.
3.note: A handshake happening and traffic flowing are two different things. Go to `wg-handshake-ok-no-traffic` now and verify the real claim with `/ping 10.20.0.1`.

wg-handshake-ok-no-traffic.seen: The WireGuard handshake is showing but the dashboard still reports the router offline / RADIUS is timing out.

0.cause: The handshake happened but no data is crossing the tunnel. The most common reason: the peer's `allowed-address` does not cover the hub's tunnel subnet, or the router's own tunnel IP was never put on `wg-cloudguest`.
0.note: `allowed-address` must contain `10.20.0.0/24` (or whatever tunnel subnet was in the script). A `last-handshake=` only means the keys matched -- routing is a separate thing. So never trust a dashboard "handshake OK", always run this ping.

1.cause: There is no address on the tunnel interface, so the router has no connected route for `10.20.0.0/24` at all.
1.note: The right `<n>` comes from this router's management IP in Router Fleet -- put in the wrong number and you clash with another router. Do not guess, look it up in the dashboard.

2.cause: The tunnel is working completely. The reason for dashboard-offline or RADIUS-timeout is somewhere else.
2.note: If the dashboard says offline, look at `router-offline-in-dashboard` (usually an NTP/clock problem). If RADIUS is timing out, go to `radius-counters` -- the tunnel is no longer a suspect.

3.tell: Sometimes a reply, sometimes a timeout (`packet-loss=50%` sort of thing).
3.cause: The uplink is flapping, or two default routes are fighting each other.
3.note: If you see an extra 0.0.0.0/0 route without a `cloudguest-` comment (created by RouterOS's own dhcp-client), remove it -- it fights with our check-gateway route.

wg-firewall-rule-order.seen: The tunnel comes up but nothing reaches the router from the hub -- WinBox/API will not open through the tunnel.

0.tell: The row number of `cloudguest-fw-allow-wg-mgmt` is HIGHER than `cloudguest-fw-drop-wan-input` (i.e. it is below it).
0.cause: RouterOS runs rules top to bottom. The drop rule matches first, so the tunnel's accept never runs at all.
0.note: This happens when the Firewall chunk was pasted AFTER the WireGuard chunk. After the move the allow rule's number must be the smaller one. Look only at the number, nothing else.

1.tell: There is no `cloudguest-fw-allow-wg-mgmt` line at all.
1.cause: The WireGuard chunk was never pasted, or only its firewall part failed to run.
1.note: `place-before=` is essential -- a plain `add` always appends to the end of the list, which means below the drop rule, which means useless.

2.tell: The allow rule is above and has flag `X` (disabled) in front of it.
2.cause: The rule exists but someone disabled it while debugging in WinBox.
2.note: The `X` flag is easy to miss even when the order is right. Always look at the flags column in the print output.

3.tell: The allow rule is above, enabled, and still nothing arrives from the hub.
3.cause: It is not a firewall problem -- the tunnel is genuinely not carrying traffic.
3.note: Go to `wg-handshake-ok-no-traffic`. Do not touch anything else in the firewall.

radius-counters.seen: The guest's OTP verifies, the app shows "connected", but there is no internet.

0.tell: All four counters are `0` -- `accepts=0 rejects=0 timeouts=0 bad-replies=0`.
0.cause: Not a single RADIUS request ever reached the router. That means the hotspot's login POST was never sent -- this is a portal-side bug, not a network one.
0.note: This was the real final blocker in the 2026-08-18 outage: the portal never had `guestIdentifier` set, so the hotspot POST silently no-op'd and the router's logs stayed completely empty. Change nothing on the router -- tell the backend/portal team. Counters at `0` mean the router never saw anything at all.

1.cause: The server's reply did arrive, but RouterOS threw it away before validating it. Usually the reply carries no Message-Authenticator attribute while the router sits at `require-message-auth=yes-for-request-resp` instead.
1.note: This is NOT a reject and NOT a timeout -- it is a third, separate counter, and it is the thing that ate hours on 2026-08-18. The real fix is on the FreeRADIUS hub. Treating it as a reject and debugging credentials is wasted time.

2.cause: The request went out and no reply came back. Either the tunnel is down (the server is on a tunnel IP), or the shared secret is wrong -- on a wrong secret FreeRADIUS drops silently rather than sending a reject.
2.note: Ping fail = tunnel problem, go to `wg-handshake-ok-no-traffic`. If ping works then the secret is wrong -- re-register with `POST /radius/nas/register-external/{router_id}` and paste the `/radius` chunk in the same sitting (registering rotates the secret).

3.cause: The server saw the request, understood it, and refused. Most commonly: this router's identifier/registration does not match the backend's router record -- the request is authenticating as some other router.
3.note: This bites particularly on the second router and beyond: if the hub's `sites-enabled/default` still has router #1's identifier hardcoded, the new router does not get a 401 -- it authenticates AS router #1 and then comes back as a Reject inside an HTTP 200 on `router_id` mismatch, with nothing in the logs. This is not fixable on the router.

4.cause: RADIUS is working perfectly. The guest is being authorised.
4.note: Run `/ip hotspot active print` -- the guest should show up there. If they do and there is still no internet, the trouble is in WAN/DNS, not in auth.

5.tell: The command errors with `no such item`.
5.cause: There is no entry under `/radius` at all -- the RADIUS chunk was never pasted.
5.note: `monitor 0` means the first entry. With no entry at all the command fails on the index itself.

radius-bad-replies.seen: In `/radius monitor 0 once` the `bad-replies` counter is climbing, while `rejects` and `timeouts` are zero.

0.cause: RouterOS is demanding a Message-Authenticator attribute in the reply. FreeRADIUS's `rlm_rest`-built Access-Accept does NOT attach one by itself, so the router silently discards every reply.
0.note: This is exactly root cause #4 from 2026-08-18. The server-side fix is the real fix. Setting `require-message-auth=no` on the router to move on is only for saving a demo -- it weakens security and hides the real bug, so raise a ticket for it.

1.cause: A reply is arriving but its authenticator hash does not match -- the shared secret differs on the two sides.
1.note: A half-wrong secret gives bad-replies rather than timeouts when the server is answering. Do not click Generate between registering and pasting, or the secret changes again.

2.cause: RouterOS's default is 300ms, which is far too short for a path over the tunnel -- a late reply sometimes turns into a bad-reply/timeout.
2.note: The script sets `timeout=3s`; seeing 300ms means the entry was made by hand or survived from an older paste.

2.note: Two DHCP servers on one LAN is the nastiest field issue there is -- guests take IPs from either one at random and half of them never reach the portal. Get DHCP turned off on the old router.
